sentence: The NHS says the risk of falling can be lowered by exercises for strength and balance and by simple changes at home.
NICE guideline NG249 recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.
Keeping walkways clear, using stair handrails and wearing well-fitting, non-slip footwear are among the home-safety suggestions.
Regular eye tests are recommended, and the NHS provides free eye tests for people over 60.

The NHS lists muscle weakness that comes with age, conditions that affect mobility or balance (such as arthritis, stroke or Parkinson's), low blood pressure, side effects of some medicines, eyesight or hearing problems, and dementia among the causes of falls.
Anyone can have a fall, but it is more likely in older people or those with mobility problems.
Some medicines, especially several taken together, can cause drowsiness, light-headedness, faintness or unsteadiness.
The NHS advises speaking to a GP or pharmacist if medicines might be affecting balance.

Postural hypotension is a drop in blood pressure that usually happens shortly after standing up from lying or sitting, and NICE includes a lying and standing blood pressure check in its falls assessment.
The NHS says regular exercises for strength and balance can improve strength and balance and reduce the risk of falls.
It lists walking and dancing, and notes evidence that regular tai chi can reduce the risk of falls.
Programmes are described as best when tailored to the individual and overseen by a trained professional.
Suggestions include keeping walkways clear, using handrails on stairs, and wearing non-slip, well-fitting footwear.
Regular eye tests are recommended, and free NHS eye tests are available to people over 60.
NICE guideline NG249 covers falls assessment and prevention in older people and in people aged 50 and over at higher risk, and recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.
The NHS lists the GP's role as checking for problems such as muscle weakness, osteoporosis and eyesight problems, and reviewing medicines.
Some areas have a falls team that offers a full assessment to older people who have fallen or are at high risk, and availability varies, so a GP can say what exists locally.
Advice after a fall includes calling for help, using a lifeline alarm if there is one, and keeping warm by covering up with a rug, blanket or towel.
It also includes moving the parts of the body that do not hurt, and getting up gradually if able.
Someone who is hurt or cannot get up should seek medical help.
